q: For how many years, Quli Qutb Shah ruled in Andhra?
explanation:
Most books and keys: 31 years (1512–1543). Strictly, formal independence came in 1518 (NextGen Qutb Shahis p.1), which gives 25 years.
Counted from 1512, when he began to rule Golconda as a virtually independent Bahmani governor, to his murder in 1543, Sultan Quli ruled 31 years. NextGen's formal independence date of 1518 gives only 25 years, which is not an option.

notes.text: - **How long Quli Qutb Shah ruled:** **31 years** (1512–1543; Deputy EO screening). ⚠ From formal independence (1518) it is only 25 years.

q: Who among the following was also called 'Malkibharam'?
explanation: Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah, the great patron of Telugu poets, was praised as 'Malkibharama' by his subjects. Muhammad Quli wrote as 'Maani'; Abul Hasan was 'Tana Shah'.

notes.text: - **Malkibharama / Malikibharam:** **Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah** (G1 2002; G1 PYQ) – a title from his subjects for tolerant rule; coinage does not explain it.

q: Which of the following was built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah?
explanation:
As printed ('was built by'), three options are right; the key (Golconda) answers the original question 'which was NOT built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah'.
The stem lost its 'NOT': Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built Hyderabad city (1591), the Charminar and the Jama Masjid, but Golconda fort existed long before him (Kakatiya mud fort 'Mankal', rebuilt by Sultan Quli and Ibrahim), so Golconda is the one he did not build.

notes.text: - **Built by Muhammad Quli:** **Hyderabad city, Charminar, Jama Masjid** – **not Golconda** fort, which was a Kakatiya fort (Mankal) rebuilt by Sultan Quli and Ibrahim (G1 2003).

q: Who of the following was the last king of the Qutub Shahi dynasty of Golkonda?
explanation: Abul Hasan Tana Shah (1672–1687) was the last Qutb Shahi ruler; Aurangzeb took Golconda in 1687 and sent him to Daulatabad.

notes.text: - **Last king:** **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** (G1 PYQ) – title "Tanisha" from Sufi saint Shah Raju Qattal.

q: Who of the following is also known as Malikibharam?
explanation: Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah was hailed as Malkibharama by his subjects for his tolerant rule and patronage of Telugu poets; Nizam-ul-Mulk, Abul Hasan and Muhammad Quli had no such title.

notes.text: - **Malkibharama / Malikibharam:** **Ibrahim Quli Qutb Shah** (G1 2002; G1 PYQ) – a title from his subjects for tolerant rule; coinage does not explain it.

q: From where did the Qutb Shahis rule?
explanation: The Qutb Shahis ruled from Golconda, their capital from 1518 (Muhammad Quli moved the court to the new city of Hyderabad in 1592). Mysore and Madras were never theirs.

notes.text: - **"From where did the Qutb Shahis rule":** **Golconda** (G2-B 1991). **Golconda today** lies in **Hyderabad** (MPPSC 1990).

q: In which year did Mohammad Qulikuthubsha ascend the Golconda throne?
explanation: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah ascended the throne in 1580 at the age of 14 and ruled till 1612. 1518 is the dynasty's foundation and 1591 the founding of Hyderabad.

q: Who was the author of the book Bangab Nama or The Book of the Pot Smoker, who lived in the Islamic Sultanate of Bijapur in Medieval Deccan?
explanation: The Bangab Nama ('Book of the Pot Smoker'), a long Dakhni poem in praise of bhang, was written by Mahmud Bahri of Bijapur; Ibrahim Adil Shah II wrote the Kitab-i-Nauras, and Namdev was a Marathi saint.

notes.text: - **Bangab Nama** ("Book of the Pot Smoker"), a Dakhni poem praising bhang, was written by **Mahmud Bahri** of Bijapur (G1 PYQ) – not either Ibrahim Adil Shah or Namdev.

q: Which of the following is not true about Gol Gumbaz?

There is no mosque and no arches near the tomb
Its dome is one of the largest of its kind

notes.text: - **⚠ NOT true:** "there is **no mosque and no arches** near the tomb" – the complex has a **mosque** and arches (G2 2003; AP History PYQ).

q: Which Muslim kingdom came into existence after the disintegration of the Bahmani Empire?
explanation: The Bahmani kingdom split into five: Adil Shahi (Bijapur), Nizam Shahi (Ahmadnagar), Qutb Shahi (Golconda), Barid Shahi (Bidar) and Imad Shahi (Berar), so all three listed kingdoms came out of it.

notes.text: - The **Bahmani** kingdom (Hasan Gangu, 1347, Gulbarga) split into **five** successor states – so Adil Shahi, Nizam Shahi and Qutb Shahi all came out of it (**all of the above**).

q:

q:
Which of the following geographical factors contributed significantly to the establishment and growth of the Vijayanagar Empire?

1. The rocky terrain of Hampi provided natural fortification and aided in defense.

2. Proximity to the Tungabhadra River ensured water supply for agriculture and urban life.

3. The coastal location of Vijayanagar allowed direct trade with the Roman Empire.

4. Availability of granite enabled the construction of grand temples and forts.

5. Godavri belt Gold reserves used for coins making.
explanation: Hampi's granite hills gave natural defence (a hill fort with seven ramparts), the Tungabhadra gave water and local granite built the temples and forts, so 1, 2 and 4. Vijayanagara was inland, not coastal, Rome had long gone, and it had no Godavari gold reserves.

notes.text: - **Abdur Razzaq**, Persian envoy of **Shah Rukh**, came in **1443** in **Devaraya II's** reign (BPSC 2018; APPSC JL 2004; UDA/LDA 2010) – not Devaraya I, Krishnadevaraya, Achyuta Raya or Vira Vijaya; described diamond bazaars, about **300 ports**, taxed **prostitution**.

q: Which king of Vijayanagara settled the quarrel between Jains and Vaishnavas?
explanation: Bukka I settled the dispute between the Jains and the Vaishnavas in 1368 (Shravanabelagola inscription) and protected the Jains. Devaraya I/II, Harihara I, Saluva Narasimha and Krishnadevaraya did not.

notes.text: - **First to enlist Muslims at all:** **Devaraya I** (NextGen; APPSC) – Devaraya II enlarged it to 10,000.

q: The "Mathura Vijayam" was written by?
explanation: Madhura Vijayam was written in Sanskrit by Gangadevi (Gangamba), wife of Kumara Kampana, on his conquest of Madurai. Molla, Tirumalamba, Ramabhadramba, Madhuravani, Polamamba and Krishnadevaraya are wrong.

notes.text: - **Title Gajabetekara** (Gajabetegara, "**hunter of elephants**") (RPSC 2010; APPSC) – it is a **title of Devaraya II**, not a coin, a king's name or a Jain monk; coins bearing it are his **Gajabetekara coins** – not Devaraya I, Bukka I or Mallikarjuna. **Andhra Bhoja** and **Dakshinapatha-swami** are Krishnadevaraya's titles.

q: Harihara and Bukka belonged to the ____ Dynasty.
explanation: Harihara and Bukka, sons of Sangama, founded the Sangama dynasty, the first of the four Vijayanagara dynasties. Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu came later; the Hoysalas were not a Vijayanagara dynasty.

q: Devaraya II, undoubtedly the greatest ruler of the Vijayanagar empire, took to the throne in 1426. Which of the following dynasties does he belong to?
explanation: Devaraya II, the greatest Sangama king, belonged to the Sangama dynasty (1336-1485). The Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu dynasties came after 1485.

notes.text: - Completed the capital; title **Vedamarga Pratishthapaka**; took **Srisailam** and **Dupadu** (near Markapur); general **Saluva Mangu** killed the Madurai Sultan → title **"Parapakshi Saluva"**.

q: Sangama, the father of Harihara and Bukkaraya, the founders of the Vijayanagara Empire, was?
options: A king of Vengi Chalukya descent
explanation: The Sangama family's inscriptions trace it to the Yadava (lunar) race, so Sangama is called a Yadava. He was not a Hoysala or Vengi Chalukya king; the Kakatiya link comes only from the legend that his sons served Prataparudra of Warangal.

notes.text: - **Sangama's lineage:** the inscriptions trace the family to the **Yadava** (lunar) race – "Sangama was **a Yadava**" (APPSC G2 2005); the Kakatiya link belongs to the brothers' service story, not to Sangama's descent.

q: Sangama, the father of Harihara and Bukka, the founders of the Vijayanagara Empire, was a ________.
options: A king of Vengi Chalukya descent
explanation:
Printed key here: 'A Kakatiya chief' (from the Kakatiya-service legend). Inscriptions and the APPSC key for the same question: a Yadava.
Sangama's family is traced in its inscriptions to the Yadava (lunar) race, so 'a Yadava king' is the key (as in the same APPSC question keyed elsewhere). 'A Kakatiya chief' is wrong: only the legend says his sons served the Kakatiyas of Warangal.

q: Who among the following authored the book 'A Forgotten Empire'?
explanation: Robert Sewell wrote 'A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagar)' (1900), with the English translation of Paes and Nuniz. Ferishta was a Persian chronicler, Saletore wrote on social and political life, Burton Stein gave the 'segmentary state', Father Heras wrote on the Aravidus.

notes.text: - **'A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagar)'** (1900) = **Robert Sewell** (APPSC G2 2011 ×2, G2 Mains 2017, JA 2012) – not Ferishta, B.A. Saletore, Burton Stein, James Fergusson, Father Heras, H.G. Wells, N. Venkataramanayya or K.A.N. Sastri; it carries the English translation of **Domingo Paes** and **Fernao Nuniz**, and covers 1336-1565.
